title: The Butterfly That Barely Ages
hook: Most animals fall apart with age. Heliconius butterflies barely do — outliving close relatives several times over with little decline, hinting that lifespan is something evolution can dial up.
key_points: Heliconius butterflies live several times longer than closely related species.
Some show little physical decline with age — unusually slow aging for an insect.
Their rare pollen-feeding diet may help fuel a longer, healthier life.
Researchers suspect deeper evolutionary changes, not just diet, extend their healthspan.
That makes them a natural model for studying how long lifespans evolve.
content_html: Aging can feel like a law of nature: bodies wear out. But Heliconius butterflies — the bright, long-lived tropical species — seem to partly opt out. A new study, reported via ScienceDaily, finds they live several times longer than their close relatives, and some show little of the decline that usually accompanies old age.
extra_html: Part of the secret may be diet. Unlike most butterflies, which sip only nectar, Heliconius also feed on pollen — a richer, protein-bearing food that could help sustain a longer, healthier life. But the researchers argue diet isn't the whole story. They suspect deeper evolutionary changes have reshaped how these insects age, slowing the wear-and-tear that limits the lifespans of similar species. That makes Heliconius a useful natural model: by comparing them with shorter-lived cousins, scientists can ask which genetic and physiological tweaks let a body stay healthy for longer — questions that reach well beyond butterflies, toward the biology of aging itself.

related.title: Metamorphosis and Life Cycles
related.hook: A caterpillar becoming a butterfly is one of nature's great transformations — many animals reshape their bodies entirely as they grow up.

related.title: Natural Selection
related.hook: No designer, no goal — just heritable variation, a struggle to survive, and the slow accumulation of whatever happens to work. That's how life adapts.
